newsitem.title: UK: UK petrol sellers see no end to price war under Labour.
newsitem.headline: UK petrol sellers see no end to price war under Labour.

text.p: The U.K. retail petrol industry would welcome reforms under a Labour government but doubts that anything can reverse the cut-throat price competition that has led to an average of four filling stations closing every day, industry sources said.
Oil companies said they favoured revised taxes that they said gave an unfair advantage to the supermarkets, the only sector to show growth in the number of sites last year when 1,500 stations shut.

"What we're looking for is a fairer market in ways the treasury treats hypermarkets and ourselves," said Michael Frend, director general of the U.K. Petroleum Industry Association, which represents the big brands.
Last week, a Labour official told Reuters that its party would be "sympathetic" to implementing reforms outlined by a Parliamentary trade committee last year.

The proposals came out of hearings into whether motorists were enjoying unrealistically cheap pump prices after Esso Petroleum launched its Pricewatch campaign that promised to match its lowest-priced competitors.
British pump prices are amongst the cheapest in Europe but retail margins are also near the bottom.

"The Esso Pricewatch campaign has done irreparable damage to the U.K. market," said John Murgatroyd, finance director of Frost Group Plc, the largest independent retailer with over 600 sites selling the Save brand.
"The Labour government, if they get in, will have more things to do then look at petrol," he said. "Any action they take will be too late...They can't do anything to salvage those sites."

Frost would welcome a code of practice being drawn up through the Office of Fair Trading and the industry covering the contractual relationships between wholesalers and retailers, one of the recommendations.
A spokeswoman for Shell, the second largest retailer in Britain behind Esso with 1,706 sites, also backed reforms in the tax structure and strategic stock requirements.
"We would welcome equal excise treatment of imports and domestically refined fuel," she said.

Although retail margins have recovered from break-even levels last summer at the height of the price war, many industry analysts said the low-cost supermarkets and overcapacity would prevent a sharp recovery in downstream profits this year, regardless of which party is elected to government on May 1.

"I think practically speaking the amount (Labour) can do to prevent natural market forces taking their full effect is limited, without intervening in the marketplace and distorting it to a major degree," said Stephen Brooks, a consultant at Wood Mackenzie in Edinburgh.
